speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Deputy Speaker, on behalf of the Minister-in-charge of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), I beg to move, "That the Bill be now read a Second time." The Bill makes amendments to the Currency Act in two areas.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Second, the offence of mutilation of currency notes, to enable the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) to license companies that sell Intelligent Banknote Neutralisation Systems (IBNS) or offer cash transportation services using IBNS.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Currency Act places legal tender limits on each coin denomination that are used for payment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The current limits today are: $2 for 5-cent, 10-cent and 20-cent coins; $10 for 50-cent coins, and no limit for $1 coins.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This means that under the Act, a customer can use coins within these limits and legally the seller has to accept the payment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Legal tender limits minimise inconvenience to vendors and their waiting customers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: However, a couple of high-profile news stories surfaced in 2014 where large quantities of coins, including $1 coins, were used for payment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: One case involved the payment of close to $20,000 in coins at a car dealer's showroom.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Another involved over $1,000 worth of coins at a handphone shop at Sim Lim Square.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Thereafter, MAS received public feedback on the need to place a legal tender limit on $1 coins.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS agreed that it is useful to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: We also took the opportunity to revise the basis for setting legal tender limits.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The different value limits for different coins currently are confusing to many and not easy to remember.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Further, instead of a value limit, we should limit the number of coins used, since the processing time and effort for coin payment depends more directly on the number of coins used, and less the total value of the coins.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: So, for example, it does not make sense to set a value limit of $2 for both 20-cent coins and 5-cent coins, which means that while a customer can use up to 40 5-cent coins, he can only use 10 20-cent coins, which also adds up to $2.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: We conducted a public consultation exercise on the proposed revisions in 2017.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: There was broad support from respondents to introduce a limit for $1 coins and have a simple and uniform limit for all coin denominations that is easy to remember.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This is much simpler than the current legal tender limits.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Notwithstanding the legal tender limit, a customer and a vendor can mutually agree to transact using quantities of coins above the limit.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: But I am sure such instances will be infrequent, especially when more people switch to using electronic payment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Deputy Speaker, I will now move to the second area of amendment to support MHA's plan to allow the use of IBNS.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: IBNS is a security system installed in containers used in the transportation of currency notes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It will permanently damage or deface the currency notes housed within it when there is an attempted robbery.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This deters robbery because the loot can be easily destroyed.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: IBNS is used in many countries in the European Union.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Some companies intend to introduce IBNS services in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MHA will facilitate this so that it is available to banks and other businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: There are certain advantages, such as replacing armed Auxiliary Police Officers who are needed today to transport large amounts of cash and reducing the risk of violent crimes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This can free up scarce armed Auxiliary Police Officers for more critical operations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MHA intends to license companies that sell IBNS or offer cash transportation services using IBNS as security service providers under the Private Security Industry Act (PSIA).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It intends to obtain industry feedback to develop the licensing conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MHA and MAS will also conduct a joint education exercise to inform the public on the identification and handling of IBNS-damaged notes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Two related amendments will also be made to PSIA so as to give effect to the Currency Act amendments.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will bring convenience to retailers and consumers as the uniform limit is easy to remember and easy to implement.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Consumers do not like getting any change in 5-cent coins and because consumers do not like receiving any 5-cent coins as change, retailers are forced to deposit them into banks.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But banks, too, impose a very high transaction cost for the deposit of coins.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is very unfavourable to small business owners and is certainly not cost-effective.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We stopped minting 1-cent coins more than 15 years ago because it is no longer actively used by the public.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I believe that businesses will face an increasingly high cost to handle cash and the removal of the 5-cent coin will benefit both consumers and retailers in the long run.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government, too, would save money from minting the 5-cent coins, which are not widely used and universally disliked.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I am not sure that the 5-cent coin is universally disliked.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, there are two changes brought about by this Bill, first, relating to the legal tender of coins and, secondly, to prepare for the introduction of IBNS.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the first change regarding the legal tender of coins, section 13 of the Currency Act is being amended to introduce a uniform limit on the use of every coin.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the Bill, the limit of 20 coins will also apply to $1 coins.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the Explanatory Brief to this Bill, MAS has stated that the rationale is to have a standardised limit on all coin denominations to make it simple to remember and easier to implement.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was further stated that the Government wishes to encourage persons to use less cash for greater convenience of payments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is there a widespread situation of persons over-using such coins for payment?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to media reports last year, MAS decided to review the existing legal tender limits after two cases were reported in 2014, which the Minister also mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One case involved a mobile shop in Sim Lim Square trying to refund a customer about $1,000 entirely in coins, while the other case involved a man who left $19,000 in coins at a car dealer's showroom.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While these cases may cross the line and be considered unreasonable conduct, are such cases very common?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am also concerned as to whether certain groups of persons who tend to transact in coins will be adversely affected by the new limit.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, persons in certain occupations tend to earn their income from customers in coins, for example, hawkers of cooked food and buskers who sing for change.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Once the Bill is passed, they can no longer insist on tendering $1 coins to pay for any item over $20.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Would the change cause hardship to such persons?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some might say that these persons could always use the coin machines at banks to deposit their coins into their bank accounts and withdraw currency notes thereafter to use.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, there are Singaporeans today who do not have a bank account or are not approved by banks to have one.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second change brought by this Bill is to prepare for IBNS.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: IBNS would operate to damage or deface currency notes when it is detected that a CIT robbery is imminent, thus rendering the notes indelibly marked or altered.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Bill contains provisions to state that such notes cannot be legally used.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: IBNS is an application of primary crime prevention, by reducing the rewards of crime, or increasing the chances of detection.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The theory is that an intended CIT robbery would lose its appeal if the perpetrator knew that the loot would be rendered worthless, or that their hands or bodies would be stained with a substance that could provide forensic evidence to link them to the crime scene.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: IBNS technology has been in use for more than three decades in Europe and found in automated teller machines, vending machines and also containers for CIT movements.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If IBNS is successful in deterring CIT robberies, there will be potential spillover cost-efficiencies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: CIT, which is enhanced with IBNS, may no longer require armed guards and armoured vehicles.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This may allow redeployment of such guards and vehicles to other areas, which will alleviate the current manpower shortages in the Auxiliary Police.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are also potential savings for organisations which need CIT security, such as Town Councils, since they can save on the service fees of armed Auxiliary Police, which are relatively high.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, IBNS is just one part of the security ecosystem for CIT.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What is critical is that IBNS is accompanied by equally secure pre- and post-handling, so as not to create vulnerabilities before the cash enters an IBNS environment and after it leaves.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Overall, Sir, I am in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: At a National Day Rally not long ago, the Prime Minister heralded the advent of a cashless society in Singapore, and local e-payment businesses are experiencing robust growth.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: A recent research report by UBS highlighted that many Asian countries are implementing measures to go cashless.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: For example, the Indian government has done away with the 500-Rupee and 1,000-Rupee banknotes and the Korean Central Bank plans to stop minting coins after next year.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Technology development has increased the scope for inclusive financial services, but it can also widen the gap between the disadvantaged and mainstream society.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Disadvantaged groups often lack digital literacy and we need to pay attention to this "digital divide".

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: For example, most of the elderly habitually use cash for transactions and are unfamiliar with the various e-payment technologies and devices available.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: To them, a cashless society often signifies greater difficulty rather than convenience.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: There is need to enhance education and training for the technologically disadvantaged, as the Minister mentioned, and the Government can provide more services that promote digital literacy.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: According to a British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) report, Sweden is set to become the first cashless society in the world.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: However, in recent years, the Swedes are increasingly concerned that doing away with cash altogether may well lead to problems for the elderly and others.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: For example, most banks have stopped providing over-the-counter teller services, and shops no longer accept cash transactions.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In addition, with an open web environment and the deployment of distributed systems, the increasing prevalence of e-payment may well have other risks.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: User-profile, consumption behaviour and personal habits and preferences are increasingly collected and mined, making it harder to protect privacy.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, for the country, the society and the financial system as a whole, the concentration of payment and settlement data in the hands of a few private companies and Government agencies may well pose increased risks of disruption to the stability of the financial system or economic security.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Of course, there are obvious benefits to doing away with coins, banknotes and to go cashless in our payments and settlement, and we should continue to promote the idea of progress towards a cashless society.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: However, I hope that this cashless society will be an inclusive one, which provides our people with choices.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: I believe that different payment methods and settlement systems should be allowed to co-exist in the foreseeable future.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Even as we redouble efforts at public education to promote various non-cash payment methods, we should also permit people the choice of their preferred payment methods, including in physical currency, such as coins and banknotes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   Frequent technological advancements mean that it is important to review our policies to ensure that we are keeping up and making the most out of the available technologies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I support the prevalent use of such systems and hope to see it utilised all around Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, merchants and customers alike should not be made to accept large amounts of coins which they may not have an avenue to use, especially with more people using cashless payment methods.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Additionally, it also discourages unnecessary delays for the rest of the customers in the queue, and abuse by way of mischief.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One particular case that made media headlines was a shop in Sim Lim Square, which Ms Sylvia Lim mentioned earlier, that refunded its customer $1,010 in coins.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There was also a customer who paid $19,000 worth of coins to a car dealer to make a point.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These acts of mischief drew the attention of local media because of the huge amount of cash involved, but I believe it is not uncommon on a smaller scale.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some customers may not bear malicious thoughts, but instead they simply want to reduce the number of coins they carry and think nothing of offloading them on to a merchant.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To them, it is still money after all, and the merchant is more likely able to find a better use for the coins.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, I understand that the limit of 20 coins applies to each denomination, across all denominations, in a single transaction.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, the change in legal tender limits is not likely to result in significant changes to the way coins are used in day-to-day transactions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am pleased that this rule is maintained.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are still many vendors, and even charity organisations that receive large amounts in coins.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While I am not disputing that a service charge could be imposed, there should be a cap because, if a counting machine is used, it does not take that much time to count the coins.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And, with increasing automation, I expect that the use of the coin deposit machines will become even more prevalent.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moreover, usually the people with large amounts of coins also tend to be those who will consider the fees that they have to bear as a significant expense.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is important to recognise that coins are still a big part of payments for small businesses, like the newspaper vendors, children’s playground operators, and provision shops.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is already a challenge for them to convert to cashless payments, and I am concerned that these policies will indirectly lead to an overall reduction in coin usage and availability, which would affect their sales.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I wish to take this opportunity to emphasise the need to engage these small businesses and help them to stay relevant even as we are promoting the use of cashless methods.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister-in-charge of MAS, let me now address their questions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, on the legal tender limits for coins.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat highlighted the need to educate the public on the new legal tender limit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Currently, information on the legal tender limits for coins is published on MAS’ website.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS also explains these limits when it receives feedback from the public regarding their experience with coin payments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Now, with a formula that is a lot easier to remember, there is an opportunity for us to explore ways to further raise public awareness of the new legal tender limit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Ms Sylvia Lim have highlighted the concern that people who get most of their income in coins may have no choice but to pay in coins and they may be affected by the new legal tender limits, especially if they use the $1 coins.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Sylvia Lim went on to explain how the new limits will work in her speech.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But let me just repeat some of the facts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Further, compared to today's legal tender limits, in terms of monetary value, there is actually no change for 50-cent coins and 10-cent coins and, in fact, an increase for 20-cent coins.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is a reduction in limit for 5-cent coins, from $2 to $1.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But it is not likely to affect many existing transactions because it is very rare for customers to use so many 5-cent coins, which is a point that Mr Yee Chia Hsing raised.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked if there is a widespread situation of persons over-using coins for payment and whether this change is really necessary.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While we agree that cases of people paying with large quantities of coins are actually very few, MAS received quite a number of feedback from the public on the need to place a limit for $1 coins following the high-profile cases I mentioned earlier, and three of us mentioned it in our speeches.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it looks like we are all aware of those cases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because of that heightened awareness, a limit for $1 coins thus serves to protect more vulnerable consumers or salespersons against abuse.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I should say that it is actually very rare that people pay for goods and services with a large amount of coins.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A great majority of lower-income Singaporeans are actually employees who do not receive their income in coins.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For small vendors like hawkers who may receive a large amount of coins and small notes, they either deposit their cash or use them as change for their customers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And in the very rare incidences where someone without a bank account somehow collects income in coins and needs to purchase something with many coins for whatever valid reasons, the vendor can adopt a flexible approach and I would urge them to do so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat further expressed concern that the legal tender limits would affect the sales of small businesses, such as newspaper vendors and provision shops, where coins are still mainly used for payments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I explained, the main change is really for the $1 coins, and instances of customers using more than 20 coins for any denomination are actually very few.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Customers who are used to cash are also very likely to use notes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have even come across a report that says small vendors that switched to e-payments actually saw an increase in their business.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This Bill proposes a practical move towards a much simpler set of limits, easier to remember, and makes it easier for merchants to operate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It will not disadvantage consumers except in some very extreme, even theoretical instances.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Yee Chia Hsing asked whether the service charge imposed by banks when accepting coins can be regulated and capped.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Banks typically charge a deposit or administrative fee for coin deposits because they incur costs in handling coins.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not just the counting machines but, beyond that, there is also authentication, sorting, packing, transport.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The setting of fees and charges for banking services are commercial decisions made by banks, but MAS will keep a close watch on the fees.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS also expects banks to disclose the fees and charges for their services upfront so that businesses and consumers can make informed decisions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At the same time, MAS has set out alternatives to the banks for depositing of coins so that the public can also deposit their coins at several designated locations managed by Certis Cisco, which has been appointed to manage MAS’ coin operations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Deposit fees at these centres are at a nominal rate of $3.50 per 1,000 pieces.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are no fees for depositing 1-cent and 5-cent coins at these centres.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Third, on the removal of 5-cent coins, raised by Mr Yee Chia Hsing, MAS will hesitate to remove 5-cent coins because they are still worth something.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And if you take a look at products sold at supermarkets, convenience stores and fast-food outlets, you will see that many basic necessities like bread, eggs, beverages and so on have 5-cents in their pricing, such as $1.95 or $2.95.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is a chance that removal of 5-cent coins may lead to such items being rounded up to the nearest 10-cents!

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Chen Show Mao talked about e-payments and a cashless society and how it will inconvenience and even threaten consumers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our approach and objective are never to be a cashless society.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We think we should promote e-payment because it is convenient to use and is more efficient.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The way to do this is not to compel but to make e-payment very convenient to use.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I should add that it is not just the seniors.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In my interactions with seniors in the community – and many of them attended digital literacy courses – many of them are actually champions of e-payment and really embrace the use of e-services, such as booking their medical appointments, paying by e-payment, so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I would also encourage not just the seniors but also the young to embrace e-payment and realise the convenience of using it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Lastly, on IBNS, Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how many banks support the use of IBNS and how MHA intends to reach out to those banks which have not expressed interest.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: He also asked about the cost impact on banks from the use of such IBNS.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As pointed out by Ms Sylvia Lim, there are some advantages for doing so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: IBNS will not be made a compulsory requirement for cash transportation services, but an added option.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While banks are generally open to new technologies, banks will also need to assess, together with their service provider, the combination of technology and manpower that best fits their needs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I beg to move.
